query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys by engineering an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure with a lamellar colony structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar colony structure
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure with a lamellar colony structure
generation.mechanism: Two-hierarchical constraint effect and self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility
generation.baseline: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloys with a dual-phase lamellar colony structure
generation.boundary: Limited by the ability to control the microstructure and the resulting mechanical properties
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing conditions and resulting microstructure that will lead to improved strength and ductility are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties of eutectic high-entropy alloys with and without tailored thermo-mechanical processing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored thermo-mechanical processing does not result in improved strength and room-temperature tensile ductility, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
